front: If both parties to an agreement make a mistake, and neither is at fault, is the agreement effective?
back: No, it is void due to mutual mistake

front: If it becomes economically unfeasible for a party to perform a contract, is the contract frustrated?
back: No, unless due to an unforeseeable event. For frustration it is not sufficient for the job to be more difficult, it must be a fundamentally different job from what was contemplated.
notes: Davis Contractors v Fareham [1956]: Contract to build houses ran way over budget due to materials and labour shortages.

front: If a secured creditor sells the charged assets for more than it is owed, what happens to the surplus?
back: Paid to the trustee/liquidator

front: If A has a contractual obligation to B, can he use the performance of that obligation as consideration for a contract with C?
back: Yes

front: If a case is accepted by the magistrates' court, is the defendant safe from any sentence greater than 12 months?
back: No - the magistrates can find him guilty then commit him to the Crown Court for sentencing

front: An additional loan is tacked onto Mortgage A after Mortgage B has been registered. What is the priority of the additional loan?
back: If Lender B had notice and agreed, the additional loan has priority. Otherwise, Mortgage B has priority.

front: Member A wishes to transfer his shares to B but is blocked by the board. What are his options?
back: Board has absolute discretion under the MAs so he has to amend by SR to complete the transfer.Otherwise he can hold the shares in trust for B indefinitely.

front: A tries to sell B a fake Picasso, but B refuses to buy it. C overhears their conversation by chance, and buys the painting. He later discovers it is fake. Can he sue A for misrepresentation?
back: Amazingly, no. A intended to induce B, not C.

front: If A conducts due diligence but does not discover B's negligent or innocent misrepresentation, can A claim against B?
back: Yes, but A's claim may be limited to the extent that he relied on B's statement.
notes: e.g. rescission may not be possible; damages may be partial / Case law here is very inconsistent.

front: If damage is foreseeable in kind, but the amount of damage that arises in fact was unforeseeable, is there legal causation?
back: Yes.
notes: e.g. If a fire is foreseeable, then there is full liability whether it's one house or the whole town.

front: What are the main examples of zero-rated supplies?
back: (1) Non-catering food(2) Water(3) Books

front: What are the requirements for the St Martin's Property exception?
back: (1) It is contemplated in the agreement that the property will be transferred to a third party / (2) It is the intention of the parties that the contract is for the benefit of the future transferee

front: What property cannot be taken by CRAR?
back: - Tools of the trade up to the first £1,350 value / - Property belonging to a sub-tenant or other third party

front: What is the required procedure at incorporation if a company is not using the MAs?
back: (1) Articles must be submitted with the application to register a company(2) Registered articles must specifically exclude or modify the MAs
notes: Failure to do (2) means the model articles are incorporated by default

front: What are the factors that must be considered for the interests of justice test?
back: (1) Is D likely to lose their liberty or suffer severe reputational damage? / (2) Significant or complex legal question? / (3) Is D unable to understand the proceedings or present their own case? / (4) Will the proceedings involve interviewing or cross-examining witnesses? / (5) Is representation in the interest of a third party other than D? /

front: How many trustees can a trust have?
back: Personalty only: 1 to ∞ / Includes realty: 2 to 4

front: What is the procedure for serving a claim outside England & Wales?
back: (1) Permission of the court must be obtained first / (2) Claimant then provides the claim form and other documents to the authorities in England & Wales / (3) Authorities in the foreign country will serve the document and provide a certificate of service

front: What are the elements of murder?
back: (1) Unlawful: No available defences (e.g. self-defence) / (2) Killing: Acceleration of death / (3) Malice aforethought: Intention to kill or cause GBH / (4) Peacetime
notes: Malice aforethought does not imply premeditation. / Foetuses cannot be murdered.

front: Can unlawful act manslaughter be committed by omission?
back: No, the unlawful act must be an intentional, positive act

front: A new client approaches a solicitor with a small transaction. Is customer due diligence required?
back: Yes. CDD is required for all new relationships.
notes: If the approach is by email and the solicitor has not met the client in person, EDD is required

front: Can a joint tenancy be severed by a will?
back: No, never

front: Do the interests of the other occupiers of a bankrupt’s house always outweigh those of the creditors?
back: No, after one year the creditors’ interests are paramount

front: A and B have a history of dealings. Sometimes A signs a rider exempting B from liability and sometimes he does not. Can B claim incorporation by consistent course of dealing on an occasion where A did not sign?
back: No, because it was not consistent whether he signed or not.

front: Can a trustee be held liable for breaches committed before his appointment?
back: No, but he is liable if he failed to properly inspect the trust documents on appointment

front: When is a claimant required to file a reply to defence?
back: When the claimant wishes to make a new matter which must be pleaded (such as misrepresentation, fraud, illegality, etc.)
notes: Otherwise optional but can be done to narrow the issues in dispute

front: How does the eggshell skull theory apply to legal causation in tort?
back: If the type of damage is foreseeable, then the extent is irrelevant, even if the claimant's own circumstances contribute to the extent

front: At what stage does the court officer provisionally assign a track to a case?
back: When the defendant files a defence
notes: The court officer then serves a notice on each party of the proposed track, including a directions questionnaire that they must return

front: What happens if a party breaches a consent order?
back: The other party has to file new proceedings in breach of contract
notes: A consent order is basically a contract

front: What is a marriage settlement?
back: A trust established on the occasion of a marriage. The partners and their children are deemed to have given marriage consideration, so the trust is enforceable even if incompletely constituted

front: When can damages be claimed in contract for loss of reputation?
back: Only by an ex-employee against his former employer whose bad reputation affects his career prospects

front: When would a court make a wasted costs order?
back: When the legal representatives' own poor conduct has caused the costs to arise

front: What is a fixed trust?
back: A trust where each beneficiary is entitled to a specific share of the trust property

front: What can a member do with a 50% shareholding?
back: Block an ordinary resolution

front: What is the biggest difference between mediation and arbitration?
back: Arbitration is binding and precludes subsequent litigation in court.

front: When and how can a party apply for pre-action disclosure?
back: When a party suspects that the other side is deliberately withholding a document that could have a material impact on the pre-action process, they can request an interim order (form N244) to disclose a specific document or class of documents.
notes: Must show in the witness statement that the other party would be required to disclose this document at trial anyway, and that it is desirable to disclose it before trial

front: What is an 'assent' by an executor or administrator?
back: A transfer of estate property to a beneficiary.
notes: An assent of land must be in writing and name the beneficiary. No rules for assents of personalty but it's nice to have them in writing.
